29.title: Three palaces
29.hook: one for the rains, one for winter, one for summer; "I was delicately nurtured" (AN 3.38)
29.howItsDone: Buddhists retell the Buddha's sheltered youth as the setting for his going forth; the Sukhamala Sutta, where he describes it, is studied as a teaching on the three intoxications of youth, health and life.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the swan, and the court that gave it to the boy who saved it. Your line was life belongs to who protects it. What small life did you care for? Day twenty-nine.

segments.voice: A new week, and a new part of the story: the palace. Remember Kondañña's one raised finger, and the king who hoped his son would stay home and rule? This is where the king acts on that hope. If the boy is going to leave because he sees the world's pain, the reasoning goes, then make sure he never sees it. Wrap him in so much comfort that he never has a reason to look past the garden wall. And for years, it works. Today, in the Buddha's own words, what it was like to grow up that way.
screen: `A NEW WEEK: THE PALACE.` → `A FATHER'S PLAN.` → `SO MUCH COMFORT, NO REASON TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: In one of the discourses, the Buddha looks back on his youth. He says he was raised delicately. Extremely delicately. His father had lotus ponds made just for him, one of blue lotuses, one of red, one of white. His clothes were made of the finest cloth from Benares. A white parasol was held over him day and night, so that cold and heat, dust and grass and dew wouldn't touch him. And he had three palaces. One for the cold season, one for the hot season, one for the rainy season. During the four months of rain, he says, he stayed up in the rainy-season palace, surrounded by musicians, and never once came down. Even the servants in his father's house ate fine rice and meat, where in other houses servants got broken rice and sour gruel. It's a remarkable thing for a teacher to say about himself. No humble origin story. He was the richest kid in town, and he tells you so. But then, in the same passage, the tone changes. He says: amid all that, a thought came to him. Ordinary, untaught people see someone old, and they're disgusted, forgetting that they'll grow old too. The same with sickness. The same with death. And when he saw that, he says, the pride of youth, the pride of health, the pride of being alive, all fell away from him. The three palaces kept out the rain, the heat, the cold. They couldn't keep out that thought. Comfort isn't a bad thing. But it can be a wall. And walls, sooner or later, have gates.

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Let the breath settle. Then look around for one comfort you forgot you had. A roof in the rain. Warm water from a tap. A chair that holds you. Glasses that let you see. Notice it, the way the Buddha noticed his palaces. Feel a little gratitude for it. Then gently ask: is there anything it's keeping me from seeing? You don't need an answer. Just let the question sit beside the gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Three palaces. One for the cold, one for the heat, one for the rains: the comfort the Buddha grew up in, and the thought that got through anyway.

30.title: Yasodhara
30.hook: the marriage; in the stories she is his equal, and later a nun in her own right
30.tomorrow: The first sight: an old man
30.howItsDone: Buddhists remember Yasodhara as the Buddha's wife and the mother of Rahula, and in many traditions as a nun and arahant; her story is told in temple art, festivals and verse, and some communities honor her especially as a model of steadfast practice.

screen: `DAY THIRTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: three palaces, one for every season, and a thought that got through the walls. Your line was comfort can be a wall. Which comfort did you step outside? Day thirty.
screen: `THREE PALACES — COMFORT CAN BE A WALL.`

segments.voice: In a lot of old stories, the princess is a prize. The hero wins a contest, and she's handed over at the end like a trophy. She barely speaks. We never find out what she thought. At first glance, the Buddha's story looks like that too. At sixteen, the tellings say, the prince is married to a beautiful young woman of the Sakya clan. There's even a contest of skill in some versions. But keep reading, and she refuses to stay a trophy. She has a name, a history of her own, and a path that becomes hers. Today, the woman beside him.
screen: `IN OLD STORIES, THE PRINCESS IS A PRIZE.` → `A MARRIAGE AT SIXTEEN.` → `SHE REFUSES TO STAY A TROPHY.`

segments.voice: Her name is Yasodhara. Yasa means glory, fame. Dhara means one who bears, who holds. The one who carries glory. And here's the first surprising thing: in the oldest texts she's barely named at all. The monastic rules usually call her simply Rahula's mother, after the son she'll have soon. It's the later tellings that bring her forward, and when they do, they make her his equal. The commentaries say she was born on the same day as him. The Jataka stories say the two of them were together across many past lives, and that long ago, when the future Buddha first vowed to seek awakening, she vowed to walk beside him, life after life. Not a prize he won. A partner who chose. And her story doesn't end with the marriage, or with his leaving, which is coming in a few days. Much later, after the Buddha has been teaching for years, Yasodhara leaves the palace too. She joins the order of nuns, and the tradition remembers her becoming fully awakened, an arahant, in her own right. There are verses said to be hers, looking back on her own long journey. Different Buddhist communities tell her story in different ways, and some modern writers have gone further, retelling the whole life from her side. That's fair, because the old sources leave a lot unsaid, and it's honest to say so. What we can say is this. The tradition that kept her remembered her as more than a wife left behind. She walked the same path, and reached the same end.

31.title: The first sight: an old man
31.hook: on a chariot ride with Channa he sees a man bent with age and asks, will this happen to me
31.carry: this is coming for all of us
31.tomorrow: the second sight: a sick man
31.howItsDone: Buddhists retell the four sights as the beginning of the Buddha's search, and many reflect regularly on the fact that they too are subject to aging, one of the five daily remembrances recited in many monasteries.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yasodhara: in the stories she is the prince's equal, and one day a nun in her own right. Your line was partner, not prize. Who did you honor as an equal? Day thirty-one.
screen: `YASODHARA — PARTNER, NOT PRIZE.`

segments.voice: Think of the oldest face you know well. A grandmother, a neighbor, the man who has run the corner shop for forty years. Now picture never having seen a face like that. Not once. The stories say the young prince grew up exactly that way. His father, remembering the prophecy that his son might leave and become a teacher, kept every sad thing out of sight. Three palaces, music, gardens, young and beautiful people everywhere. Then one day the prince asks his charioteer, Channa, to drive him out to the park. The road has been swept and decorated. And still, at the side of it, there stands a man. Today, the first of four things the prince was never meant to see.
screen: `THE OLDEST FACE YOU KNOW.` → `A PALACE WITH NO OLD FACES.` → `A MAN BY THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: The man is bent almost double. Gray hair, few teeth, leaning on a stick, trembling as he walks. The prince has never seen anything like him. What is wrong with that man, he asks. His hair isn't like other people's hair. His body isn't like other bodies. Channa answers plainly: that is what we call an old man. And the prince asks the question the whole story turns on. Will this happen to me? Channa doesn't soften it. Yes. To you, to me, to everyone. Nobody gets past old age. The prince tells him to turn the chariot around. No park today. He goes home and sits alone with it. Here's something most people never hear. In the oldest Pali texts, this story of the four sights is told about a Buddha from long ago, named Vipassi. The later biographies, written centuries after the Buddha, tell it about Siddhattha, and that's the version the whole Buddhist world now knows. The Buddha's own memory in the suttas is quieter. He remembers being a young man in comfort and noticing that people feel disgust at someone old, forgetting they will be old too. When he saw that, he says, the pride of youth simply fell away. Either way, the point is the same. The prince didn't learn a new fact. Everyone knows people grow old. What changed is that he let it mean him. Old age stopped being something that happens to other people. That shift, from them to me, is where Buddhists say the path begins to open.
screen: `WHAT IS WRONG WITH THAT MAN?` · `WILL THIS HAPPEN TO ME?` · `A STORY TOLD OF AN OLDER BUDDHA.` · `FROM THEM TO ME.` · then, large: `THIS IS COMING FOR ALL OF US.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one old face you know. Look at it slowly, the way the prince looked from the chariot. The lines around the eyes. The hands. Now let a quiet thought arrive: this face was once young, like mine. And my face is on its way to being old, like this one. Don't turn it into fear. Just let the two faces sit side by side, kindly. If there is gratitude for this person, let it come. The bell holds the time.
The first sight. An old man by the road, and a prince asking, will this happen to me. The first of four sights that turned his life around.
screen: `THE FIRST SIGHT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: this is coming for all of us. Today, look kindly at one old face, in a shop, on a bus, in a photo, and let it be a face you're on your way to. Day thirty-one.

32.title: The second sight: a sick man
32.hook: a man shaking with fever by the road; and this too, he asks
32.tomorrow: the third sight: a dead man
32.howItsDone: Many Buddhists recite the five remembrances, which include being subject to illness, and in some traditions monks visit and chant for the sick, reminding everyone present that illness is part of every life.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first sight: an old man by the road, and the prince asking, will this happen to me. Your line was this is coming for all of us. Whose old face did you look at kindly? Day thirty-two.
screen: `THE FIRST SIGHT — THIS IS COMING FOR ALL OF US.`

segments.voice: You know the morning. You wake up and something is off. A scratch in the throat, a heaviness behind the eyes. Yesterday you had plans. Today the plans belong to the fever. Nobody asked you. The body simply decided. The stories say the prince went out a second time. The king had doubled the guards and the music, hoping to keep his son's mind on pleasure. Channa drove the chariot out again, down a road swept clean. And by the side of it lay a man shaking with fever, too weak to stand, being helped up by others. The prince looked, and asked the question again, a little quieter this time. Today, the second sight.
screen: `THE MORNING YOU WAKE UP SICK.` → `A SECOND RIDE.` → `A MAN SHAKING BY THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: What's wrong with him, the prince asks. Channa tells him: this man is sick. And again the question: can this happen to me? And again the plain answer: to everyone. Nobody is beyond sickness. The first sight was about time, the slow bending of age. This one is sharper. Sickness doesn't wait for old age. It can arrive at twenty, at five, on a Tuesday, in the middle of your plans. The prince had thought of his body as his, the way a palace was his. The fever by the road said otherwise. The body does what it does. Years later, the Buddha put it in a line that surprises people. This body, he told his monks, isn't yours, and it doesn't belong to anyone else either. It's the result of old causes, something to be seen clearly, not owned. That's the heart of today's line. The body is borrowed. Not a prison, not a possession. A loan, looked after for a while, returned in the end. And the Buddha lived what he taught. Near the end of his life, sick and in pain, he told his friend Ananda that his body was like an old cart that keeps going only because it's held together with straps. He didn't pretend. He didn't despair either. Buddhists say this is the point: to see sickness as it is, without the extra layer of shock, why me, how dare you. The fever is real. The outrage is the part you might be able to set down.
screen: `CAN THIS HAPPEN TO ME?` · `SICKNESS DOESN'T WAIT FOR AGE.` · `NOT YOURS, NOT ANYONE ELSE'S.` · `AN OLD CART HELD WITH STRAPS.` · then, large: `THE BODY IS BORROWED.`

segments.voice: Settle into your seat and let the breath find its own pace. Now look for one small ache. A stiff neck, a sore knee, tired eyes. Everyone has one somewhere. Rest your attention on it, gently, the way you'd rest a hand on a friend's shoulder. Notice it without the story. Not, this always happens, not, why won't it stop. Just the sensation itself: warm, tight, dull, moving. If the ache changes, let it. If your mind runs off, come back to it. The bell holds the time.
The second sight. A sick man by the road, and the prince learning that illness comes to everyone, at any age, without asking.
screen: `THE SECOND SIGHT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the body is borrowed. Today, when some part of you aches or tires, try thanking it instead of scolding it, the way you'd treat something lent to you by a friend. Day thirty-two.

33.title: The third sight: a dead man
33.hook: a funeral procession, the mourners weeping; the prince goes quiet
33.howItsDone: In many Buddhist monasteries the five remembrances are chanted daily, and Buddhists often reflect on death (maranasati) as a regular practice, sometimes at funerals where monks chant on impermanence.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second sight: a man shaking with fever, and the prince learning illness comes at any age. Your line was the body is borrowed. Did you thank an aching part instead of scolding it? Day thirty-three.
screen: `THE SECOND SIGHT — THE BODY IS BORROWED.`

segments.voice: Most of us have a first funeral we remember. The smell of the flowers. The shoes that pinched. An adult you'd never seen cry, crying. Maybe you didn't understand it all, but you understood that something in the room could not be fixed. The prince had never had that day. Now, on a third ride out, Channa's chariot meets a crowd coming the other way. People in mourning clothes, weeping, some beating their chests. On their shoulders they carry a bier, and on the bier lies a man wrapped in cloth, perfectly still. The prince watches them pass. He doesn't speak for a while. Today, the third sight.
screen: `YOUR FIRST FUNERAL.` → `A CROWD COMING THE OTHER WAY.` → `THE PRINCE GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: When he finally asks, the question is simple. What is that? Channa says: that is a dead man. He will not see his mother or father again, and they will not see him. And the prince asks the same question as before, but this time it lands differently. Will I die too? Yes. Everyone. Old age was slow. Sickness was sudden. Death is final. In the old stories he rides home shaken, and in some tellings he cries out that it's shameful to be born, if this is where birth leads. Notice what the third sight adds. It isn't only about my death. The mourners are the other half of the scene. Everyone we love will go, and we will go from them. That's why this sight hits hardest. Buddhists have a practice that comes straight from this moment. The Buddha taught five things worth remembering every day, and many monasteries chant them each morning. I'm of the nature to grow old. I'm of the nature to become sick. I'm of the nature to die. Everything and everyone dear to me will change, and I'll be parted from them. My actions are the only thing I truly own. It can sound bleak. Buddhists who say these every day often report the opposite. The remembrances don't make life darker. They make it vivid. The phone call you meant to make. The person across the kitchen table, who will not always be there. The Pali word for death is marana, and the Buddha's teaching is that looking at it, calmly, is how you stop wasting the time you have.
screen: `WHAT IS THAT?` · `THE MOURNERS ARE HALF THE SCENE.` · `FIVE THINGS TO REMEMBER DAILY.` · `NOT DARKER. VIVID.` · then, large: `EVERYONE WE LOVE WILL GO.`

segments.voice: Find a comfortable seat and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one person you have lost. It might be recent, it might be long ago. It might even be someone still living, whom you lost in another way. Say their name, inside or out loud. Let a picture of them come: a laugh, a coat, a way they said your name. You don't need to do anything with the feeling. Just let them be remembered. If tears come, let them. If gratitude comes, let that too. The bell holds the time.
The third sight. A funeral on the road, and the prince learning that death comes to everyone, and parts everyone from those they love.

34.title: The fourth sight: a wanderer
34.hook: a shaven man in a robe, owning nothing, calm
34.carry: there is another way to live
34.howItsDone: Buddhist monks and nuns today still follow the samana's way of life in many places, shaving their heads, wearing robes and receiving food as alms, and lay Buddhists often honor them as living examples of another way to live.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third sight: a funeral on the road, and the prince going quiet. Your line was everyone we love will go. Who did you call or message? Day thirty-four.
screen: `THE THIRD SIGHT — EVERYONE WE LOVE WILL GO.`

segments.voice: Three rides, three shocks. Age, sickness, death. If the story stopped there, it would be a very sad story, and the prince might have spent the rest of his life hiding in his gardens. But there's a fourth ride. Picture the prince now, more troubled than he has ever been, looking out from the chariot. And there, walking along the road, is a man with a shaved head, in a plain robe the color of earth. He carries a bowl. He owns, as far as anyone can tell, nothing else. And his face is calm. Not cheerful, not grim. Calm, in a world that just showed the prince three reasons to despair. Today's word is what that man was.
screen: `THREE RIDES, THREE SHOCKS.` → `A SHAVED HEAD, A BOWL, A ROBE.` → `A CALM FACE.`

segments.voice: The prince asks: who is that? And Channa says, that's a samana. A wanderer, one who has gone forth. The word samana comes from a root that means to strive, to make an effort. In the Buddha's India there were many of them: men, and some women, who left home, gave up property and family life, and walked the roads looking for the answer to exactly the questions the prince had just been asking. Why do we age? Why do we suffer? Is there a way out? They lived on what people put in their bowls, slept in forests and caves, and argued with each other in the town squares. The samanas weren't one group. There were many teachers and many paths. The Jains, whose tradition is still alive today, came from this same world. So did the Buddha himself: for the rest of his life, outsiders would call him the samana Gotama. Here's the heart of the fourth sight. The first three were questions. The fourth was a possibility. The prince had just learned that age, sickness and death come for everyone, palace or no palace. And here was someone who had looked at the same facts and was not afraid. The stories say something in the prince went still and bright. Not an answer yet. Just the sense that there is another way to live, and that someone, somewhere, is already living it. That sense, that another way exists, is where every search begins.

Now, gently, let your own face do a little of the same. Soften the jaw. Let the eyes rest. You're not pretending. You're just letting calm be possible for a minute. The bell holds the time.

35.title: A son is born
35.hook: news of his son arrives; the child is named Rahula, "a fetter"
35.carry: love, and the fear inside it
35.howItsDone: Buddhists tell the story of Rahula's birth as part of the going forth, and Buddhist parents are taught to love fully while practicing non-attachment, which means not clinging, rather than not caring.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth sight: a samana, a calm wanderer with a bowl. Your line was there is another way to live. Whose calm face did you find? Day thirty-five, the last day in the palace week.
screen: `SAMANA — THERE IS ANOTHER WAY TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: Anyone who has held a newborn knows the feeling. The love arrives all at once, enormous. And right behind it, sometimes in the same breath, comes something else. What if something happens to this child? You've never had so much to lose. In the stories, the prince is riding home from the park, the fourth sight still shining in his mind, when a messenger reaches him. Yasodhara has given birth. You have a son. And the prince, the stories say, answers with a strange sentence. Not a cheer. Something closer to a sigh. Today's word is the name that came from it.
screen: `THE LOVE ARRIVES ALL AT ONCE.` → `SO MUCH TO LOSE.` → `A MESSENGER ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: What the prince says, in the later telling, is: a rahula is born, a fetter is born. A bond. Something that ties me down. When the king hears it, he names the baby Rahula. It sounds harsh to modern ears, and people read it in more than one way. Some hear a father torn: he has just glimpsed another way to live, and now there's a child holding him to this one. Others hear simple honesty about love. The prince doesn't say the baby is bad. He says the love is binding, which every parent knows is true. And scholars add a note: the name may once have meant something else, perhaps tied to Rahu, the shadow that swallows the moon in an eclipse, and the fetter story may explain a name that came first. The traditions also tell the timing differently. In the Pali commentaries, Rahula is born the day his father leaves. In some northern Buddhist tellings, he's born years later, on the night of the awakening. The sources disagree, and that's fine to say. What today's word holds is the feeling underneath. Love, and the fear inside it. Buddhism doesn't say stop loving. It says look closely at the gripping, the part that wants to hold so tight nothing can ever change. And Rahula doesn't vanish from the story. He comes back, and the Buddha himself will teach him. That's a story for later. Now look back at this week: three palaces, Yasodhara, four sights, and a son. Everything the prince has, and everything he is about to leave.
screen: `A RAHULA IS BORN — A FETTER.` · `A FATHER TORN, OR PLAIN HONESTY?` · `THE SOURCES DISAGREE.` · `LOVE WITHOUT GRIPPING.` · then, large: `LOVE, AND THE FEAR INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: Find something you love that you can hold: a mug, a photo, a stone from a beach, your own hand. Sit with it. Now close your fingers around it tightly. Feel the grip, the tension up the arm. Stay there a breath or two. Then slowly loosen. Let it rest in an open palm. Still yours, still loved, just not squeezed. Notice the difference in your body between holding and gripping. Breathe with the open hand. The bell holds the time.
Rahula. The Buddha's son, whose name, in the old telling, means a fetter: the tie of love that holds us.
screen: `RAHULA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: love, and the fear inside it. Today, when you feel the worry that comes with loving someone, notice it, and loosen your grip by one finger. Day thirty-five.
